1284-tom-swift-and-his-air-scout-or-uncl:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift into the skies for Uncle Sam, testing a new air scout plane against spies and saboteurs who want its secrets. The tale moves through workshops, night flights, and a chase over land and sea, with Tom's inventions saving the day.

The book, written as war loomed, mixes boy's adventure with patriotic verve. Tom's pluck and his gadgets carry a brisk plot. It suits young readers who like aviation yarns and the Tom Swift formula of brains, bravery, and machines. Tom's gadgets and pluck carry a brisk, patriotic aviation yarn.
18057-flower-of-the-dusk:
Myrtle Reed wrote Flower of the Dusk in 1908, printed in New York and London by G. P. Putnam's Sons. Reed, author of Lavender and Old Lace and The Master's Violin, was a best-selling writer of gentle romance, and this novel is one of her most loved.

Chapters run from a maker of songs and Miss Mattie to the tower of Cologne, the seventh of June, Eloise, a letter, and a fairy godmother. Love, music, and late-life hope weave through the tale. Reed writes with warmth and a light, fanciful touch. It is a sweet, old romance, best for readers who like tender stories of the heart.
22158-the-lure-of-the-mask:
Harold MacGrath wrote The Lure of the Mask, a romantic novel published in 1908 with pictures by Harrison Fisher. It begins with a voice in the fog. A pleasant, idle dream of travel is broken by a singing voice so fine it seems divine. The hearer cannot rest until he finds the woman behind the mask of fog.

The search leads through Italy, masked balls, and operatic circles. MacGrath, a newspaperman turned best-selling novelist, spins romance with a light hand. Secrets of birth and old wrongs thicken the plot in his usual style. The book was popular enough to reach the early silent screen, and it still reads as smooth Edwardian entertainment.
23103-traders-risk:
Roger Dee works his crew between jumps in Trader's Risk. The crew works in haste between jumps. One Chafi throws the ship out of hyperdrive close beside a sun's lone planet. Another, on the following jump, works the charts to name the system they are crossing.

Numbered alien crewmen and a trader's thin margins give the story its working texture. Dee writes space commerce as seamanship, charts, jumps, and cargo risks in place of canvas and ports. The Chafi, birdlike crew, supply the alien flavor without slowing the plot. Readers get a compact trading voyage in the Astounding manner, brisk, technical, and quietly fond of its nonhuman hands.
27352-shapes-that-haunt-the-dusk:
Harper's Novelettes series, edited by William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden, gathered these ten eerie tales under one cover, with Harper copyrights running from 1891 to 1907. Each story is a short, self-contained visit to the uncanny, by a different hand, and the collection suits reading one tale at a time.

Georg Schock opens with The Christmas Child, in which Mary lies awake listening to a solemn clock while Conrad sleeps. Howard Pyle, Madelene Yale Wynne, Harriet Lewis Bradley, Hildegarde Hawthorne, and F. D. Millet supply further tales of haunting and return. The volume gives a good survey of the American ghost story as Harper's readers knew it.
3047-life-s-little-ironies-a-set-of-tale:
Thomas Hardy collected Life's Little Ironies, with colloquial sketches called A Few Crusted Characters, in a first collected edition of 1894, reprinted here in the 1920 Macmillan edition. The tales include The Son's Veto, For Conscience' Sake, A Tragedy of Two Ambitions, On the Western Circuit, To Please His Wife, The Melancholy Hussar, and The Fiddler of the Reels. A map of Wessex accompanies the volume.

Hardy's ironies turn on letters, vows, and timing, as a man reads a young girl's letter twice, charmed by its simple, self-possessed language and the dignity of a womanhood enough for itself. Four sides fill, with lines crossed after the fashion of former days. The collection shows Hardy's short fiction at its most concise and cruel.
32513-the-third-little-pet-book-with-the:
Aunt Fanny's Third Little Pet Book, published in New York in 1863, tells the tale of Mop and Frisk, two dogs, in words of five letters and less. The book is dedicated to her little friend Howard of Murray Hill Avenue. It opens in a small town by a lake. Frisk, a pert black and tan dog with tail bolt upright and matching ears, lives beside Mop, a shabby old cur with a broom-worn head and long drooping ears.

Contents follow the dogs leaving home, meeting once more, Mop's tale, and Frisk's tale, with Dash seeing a play, the death of poor Jack, and Frisk finding a new home. An illustration shows Mop saving Hal's life. Aunt Fanny, author of Night Caps and Mittens, writes for very young readers, using short words to make a dog story easy to read aloud and alone.
33230-the-gray-mask:
Wadsworth Camp's mystery novel follows Garth, a young man new to the detective bureau, who is called in by his inspector and shown a gray mask. The mask becomes the mark of a strange case that pulls him into a web of threats, stolen goods, and men who hide their faces and their aims. Camp builds the tale through tense talks, night work, and clues that point in more than one way at once.

As Garth digs deeper, the mask keeps turning up where he least expects it, and each new link makes the danger more plain. The novel blends police work with a puzzle plot, so the reader must weigh who can be trusted and what each masked visit means. Its pace stays brisk, and its close ties the mask, the thefts, and the men behind them into one clear chain.
6413-from-october-to-brest-litovsk:
Leon Trotzky, in an authorised 1919 translation from Russian, writes from October to Brest Litovsk, when events moved so fast that memory alone could hardly set them in order. Newspapers and documents were not at hand, and repeated breaks in the Brest negotiations created a suspense no longer bearable. The translator notes that Trotzky uses the Russian calendar, thirteen days behind the Gregorian, until near the end.

Social Revolutionists appear as S. R., maximalists for bolsheviks, and minimalists for mensheviks in the text. Peasants seize land of their own accord, land committees face arrest, and the Constituent Assembly recedes as the bourgeoisie insists on calling it only after peace. Trotzky writes revolution as argument and action, where a negotiator must also govern a country seizing its own future.
8681-the-face-and-the-mask:
Robert Barr gathers a dozen and more short stories in The Face and the Mask. Dedicated with a wink to the American minister who helped so many unknown literary aspirants that he could hardly escape a dedication. Titles set the range: The Woman of Stone, The Chemistry of Anarchy, The Fear of It. The Metamorphoses of Johnson, The Reclamation of Joe Hollands, The Type-Written Letter, and The Doom of London. An illustration shows a girl kissing the tips of her fingers.

Barr, a journalist turned storyteller, favours sharp twists, modern inventions, and moral surprises. Anarchists, new explosives, mysteries, and high-stakes games all appear, told with brisk humour. The collection shows late Victorian short fiction at its most entertaining, when magazines wanted a complete thrill in a few thousand words. Readers who like O. Henry's surprises will find a Canadian cousin here, less sentimental and often darker.
924-to-be-read-at-dusk:
Charles Dickens gathered these tales to be read at dusk, opening with five couriers sitting together, counting one, two, three, four, five. The stories that follow are ghostly and strange, told for the hour when light fails and the mind turns to shadows. The volume belongs to Dickens's shorter, darker pieces.

Dickens writes with his usual vividness, but here the mood is eerie rather than comic, and the tales linger after the telling. The collection suits readers who enjoy a chill on a winter evening, from a master who knew how to raise a ghost with a few plain words. It is a small, atmospheric Dickens set.
9849-the-brown-mask:
Percy J. Brebner wrote The Brown Mask in 1911, a romance of Monmouth's rebellion and its aftermath. Chapters follow brethren of the road, Barbara Lanison, and the nun of Aylingford, through Sedgemoor and afterwards. Mad Martin, King Monmouth, and the Jolly Farmers fill the road scenes. Barbara helps close a door, rebels, and sacrifices, on a journey to Dorchester.

Later chapters bring scarlet hangings, Lord Rosmore's terms, and a flight along the north road, as love and fear contend. Brebner writes with brisk, historical color. A reader gets a rousing tale of 1685 England, where rebels, fugitives, and brave women face the hangman.
britannica-1911-abakansk: Abakansk is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry sets the fortified town in Siberia's Yeniseisk government, on the Yenisei river south-west of Krasnoyarsk. It counts as the mildest and most healthful spot in Siberia, the entry claims. Old mounds near by hold statues of men seven to nine feet high, covered with picture writing, ascribed to the Li Kitai. Peter the Great raised a fort there in 1707. Two thousand people are counted.
britannica-1911-basilisk:
Basilisk is a name with two lives, set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. For the ancients it named a horrid monster of their imagining, the Greek basiliskos and Hebrew tsepha, credited with malignant powers and a fiendish look. 

Modern zoology borrowed the name for a real animal. It now labels a genus of lizards of the iguana family, named for a fancied likeness to the monster. Males carry an erectile crest on the head, and a higher scaly crest along back and tail. Basiliscus americanus, green and brown with dark crossbars, reaches a yard long, eats only plants, and lives by rivers in Mexico and Guatemala. At alarm it plunges from overhanging branches and runs semi-erect across the water, earning the local name pasa-rios, ferrymen.
britannica-1911-berdyansk:
Berdyansk is a seaport town of Russia, in the government of Taurida, on the north coast of the Sea of Azov. Its people grew from 12,223 in 1867 to 29,168 by 1900. Bricks and tiles, tallow and macaroni are its chief industries, plain goods for a working port.

The roads where ships anchor are sheltered from every wind but the south, which raises a heavy surf; a mole built in 1863 guards against that. Cereals, flour, wool, hemp, skins and fish go out from Berdyansk, while hardware, fruit, oil and petroleum come in. Salt lagoons lie just outside the town. The entry is a compact port record: position, shelter, trade and growth.
britannica-1911-berezovsk:
Berezovsk is a village of eastern Russia in the government of Perm, on the eastern slope of the Ural mountains. It lies eight miles north-east of Ekaterinburg. The village is the centre of a gold-mining region of the same name, a tract some five miles by twenty-two.

The Berezovsk mines have been known since 1747, which makes the field one of Russia’s oldest gold grounds. Mining is not the village’s only work. Its people also make boots, cut stone and practise cabinet-making, the joiner’s trade. The entry is a few lines long: a village, its mines, their age, and the side trades that fill out its living.
britannica-1911-bergamask: Bergamask, also written Bergomask, is a clumsy rustic dance named after Bergamo in northern Italy. It copied the country folk of that district, whose manners were reputed to be very awkward. The comedy of the dance lay in that clumsiness, played up for laughs. Shakespeare knew the form well enough to call for one in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, where the rude mechanicals perform it. The whole entry is that short note: a name, a hometown, a reputation, and a famous stage moment.
britannica-1911-blagovyeshchensk:
Blagovyeshchensk is a town in East Siberia and the chief town of the Amur government in Russia. It stands on the left bank of the Amur River near where the Zeya joins it, 610 miles by river above Khabarovsk. Founded in 1856, it held 37,368 people in 1900.

The entry is brief and factual. The town was the seat of the bishop of Amur and Kamchatka, and it had steam flour-mills and ironworks. Its trade role is spelled out in three lines of business. Tea bound for Russia passed through it, cattle came in from Transbaikalia and Mongolia, and grain trade for the Amur region centred there as well.
britannica-1911-bryansk:
Bryansk is a town of Russia in the government of Orel, 83 miles by rail west-north-west of the city of Orel, standing on the river Desna. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that it is mentioned in 1146, when it was also known as Debryansk, and that it later formed a separate principality.

That principality ended in 1356, and after the Mongol invasion the town fell to the Lithuanians before passing to the Russian empire early in the 17th century. The entry records a shipbuilding dock under the empress Anne, closed in 1739, an arsenal for founding cannon from 1783, and a cathedral built in 1526. Its works turned out iron, rope, brick and tallow, and its population grew from 13,881 in 1867 to 23,520 in 1897.
britannica-1911-chelyabinsk:
Chelyabinsk is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Russia, in the government of Orenburg. It stands at the east foot of the Urals. It is the head of the Siberian railway. Samara lies 624 miles away by rail to the west south west, and Ekaterinburg 154 miles to the north north west. The town's population in 1900 was 25,505. It was founded in 1658.

The entry gives the town's work in a few lines. Tanneries and distilleries operate there. Chelyabinsk is the centre of the trade in corn and cattle produce for the Ural iron works. Its place at the foot of the mountains and at the rail head made it the market where farm goods from the steppe met the mining and iron country of the Urals. The whole account is brief, but it fixes the town's role as a junction of railway, farm trade, and industry.
britannica-1911-damask:
The hosted text opens partway through its account of damask, in mid-sentence on the kinds of yarn used. What survives describes a figured cloth, usually of flax or tow yarns and sometimes part cotton. The finest grades use the best linen yarn and come out pure white. Pattern shows by long floats of warp and weft set at right angles. Those floats catch the light unevenly, so the design shifts with the viewer.

Shorter floats give softer effects, and double damask weaves give the finest results of all. Any subject, however intricate, can be woven this way if cost is no bar. Belfast and Dunfermline lead the British making of fine damasks. Cotton damasks from Paisley, Glasgow, and Lancashire serve for table-cloths and toilet covers, often coloured for export markets. Silk damasks for curtains and upholstery come from the silk-weaving centres.
britannica-1911-flask:
Flask, in its earliest Old English meaning, was a vessel for carrying liquor, made of wood or leather. Current uses give the word several shapes. One is a vessel of metal or wood, once of horn, for carrying gunpowder. Another is the long-necked glass bottle in plaited straw that holds oil or Italian wine, the Florence flask. Like-shaped vessels serve in laboratories. A third is a small pocket receptacle for spirits, often leather-covered, with part of its case forming a cup.

In metal-founding, a flask is also the wooden frame holding part of a mould. The entry then treats flagon, a doublet of flask. It traces the word through medieval Latin, Italian, French and German forms. Its origin may be a reshaped Latin vasculum, though a link with flat is also weighed.
britannica-1911-kansk: Kansk is a town of eastern Siberia, in the government of Yeniseisk, 151 miles by rail east of Krasnoyarsk. It stands on the Kan River, a feeder of the Yenisei, and on the great Siberian highway. Its population in 1897 was 7504. It is the chief town of a district in which gold is found. The town lies on low ground and is subject to flooding by the river. The entry is a few lines only: place, river, road, people, gold, and the flood risk of the site.
britannica-1911-kustanaisk:
Kustanaisk is a town of Asiatic Russia, in the province of Turgai. It stands on the Tobol river, 410 miles E.N.E. of Orenburg, in a very fertile part of the steppes. In 1897 it held 14,065 people. Its first buildings rose in 1871, and it has grown since with American-like speed. Settlers from Russia built a large village there. It became the centre of the district government in 1884, and a town in 1893, first under the name Nicolaevsk and later as Kustanaisk.

The town is a centre of schooling, and a cathedral has been built. It has tanneries, tallow works and potteries, and a fair for cattle. Its trade is strong enough to make it a rival to Orenburg and Troitsk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-usk:
Adam of Usk, English priest, canonist, and chronicler, was born at Usk, Monmouthshire, between 1360 and 1365, whose death date is unknown. He studied at Oxford, took his doctorate, and became canon law's extraordinarius. He practised in Canterbury's archiepiscopal court from 1390 to 1397, and in 1399 marched to Chester with the archbishop and Bolingbroke's army.

Richard's surrender then won Adam the livings of Kemsing and Seal in Kent, then a prebend at Bangor. Bold criticisms cost him the king's favour, and he was banished to Rome in 1402; in 1404 and later he was nominated to Hereford and St. David's but could obtain neither. His Latin chronicle covering English history, 1377 to 1404, appeared through Edward Maunde Thompson as Chronicon Adae de Usk in 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asterisk:
An asterisk, from Greek aster, a star, is a liturgical utensil of the Greek rite, not used in the Roman rite at all. It is made of two curved bands, or slips, of silver or gold crossing at right angles to form a double arch. It is placed over the amnos, or morsels of blessed bread, spread on the paten during the proskomide and part of the Greek liturgy. Its purpose is to stop the veil touching or disturbing those blessed but unconsecrated particles.

It guards the bread while the paten is carried from prothesis, or preparation table, to altar, or while it stands at either place. It is set aside after the Creed, not used again in the liturgy. The asterisk is topped by a cross, often with a tiny star hung from its junction. In the Greek Orthodox church it runs larger than in the Greek Catholic church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minsk:
Minsk, suffragan of Mohileff in Western Russia, stands on the Swislotsch, a tributary of the Beresina, which flows into the Dnieper. In 1879 it numbered 91,500 inhabitants, of whom 27,280 were Catholics. It is the nominal see of a Roman Catholic, a Graeco-Ruthenian Uniat, and a Russian Orthodox bishop, a threefold claim reflecting the region's tangled religious history.

After suppressing the sees of Smolensk and Livland, Catherine II obtained from the pope the metropolitan see of Mohilew, arbitrarily abolishing the see of Kieff at the same time. To make amends, Paul I, with Pius VI's concurrence, established the diocese of Minsk, giving the area's Catholics a bishop of their own after decades of shifting jurisdictions.
doe-osti-3016062-current-best-practices-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38528, by André M Coleman, Christopher M Chini, Arielle J Catalano, and thirteen colleagues, dates to February 2026. It gathers current best practices for cutting wildfire risk from electric transmission and distribution systems. The work answers section 4(d) of Executive Order 14308 on wildfire prevention and response.

Practices span weather forecasting and monitoring, line design, operations, and planning. They aim to stop power lines from starting fires without raising costs for customers. One section explains how heat and smoke near a fire can weaken air insulation and trip a line, even without flame contact. The report was prepared for use alongside a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission technical conference on wildfire risk. Utility staff get a single reference for what good practice now looks like.
flower-of-the-dusk:
Reed writes a gentle romance in Flower of the Dusk, dated 1908. Myrtle Reed opens with a maker of songs, then brings in Miss Mattie and a chapter named for the seventh of June. Eloise follows, as the contents run on through the loves of a small circle.

The sampled pages find Allan, a doctor, at Miss Mattie's bedside. She has, in her own words, a busted back, hurt as she rose from stooping at a bureau drawer. Allan talks her out of her fears with a joke. There will be no surgical operation, no mortar piled on her to set, no striped nurses, and no plaster cast. Two pills every four hours will do. Reed's manner is warm and light, and her tale keeps its sorrows at dusk rather than at midnight.
from-october-to-brest-litovsk:
From October to Brest-Litovsk, by Leon Trotsky in an authorized translation from the Russian, is the Bolshevik leader's own account of taking power. Trotsky writes without newspapers or documents, he says. Events move too fast to set down from memory in order. The Brest-Litovsk negotiations keep breaking off, and the suspense is no longer bearable. He will recall the landmarks of the October revolution now, and correct the account later from documents.

The translator warns that dates follow the Russian calendar, thirteen days behind. Maximalist often stands for Bolshevik in the text. Trotsky opens with the middle class intellectuals in the revolution. His party, he insists, always expected power through the logic of events. The book argues while it narrates. Every meeting is also a brief for the defense. History is written by the man still fighting it.
life-s-little-ironies-a-set-of-tales-wit:
Thomas Hardy collected these tales, first gathered in 1894. Macmillan's 1920 printing lists the contents under a map of Wessex. The Son's Veto and For Conscience' Sake lead the volume. A Tragedy of Two Ambitions and On the Western Circuit follow.

To Please His Wife and The Melancholy Hussar continue the ironies. The Fidler of the Reels adds a beloved Wessex tale. A Few Crusted Characters supplies the closing colloquial sketches. Hardy's title promises small fates turned by cruel, quiet twists. The Melancholy Hussar of the German Legion marches among the tales. A Tradition of Eighteen Hundred and Four adds Napoleonic memory.
podcast-joerogan-vZEcVY2iZsk:
Jacques Vallee, one of the most respected researchers in the UFO field, joins Joe Rogan for episode 2288. Vallee is a computer scientist and astronomer who has studied the phenomenon since the 1960s. He even inspired the French scientist character in Close Encounters of the Third Kind.

Vallee brings data rather than dogma, drawing on case files he has gathered for decades. He questions the simple alien-spaceship story and points to stranger patterns in the reports. Rogan treats him as the serious elder of a field full of noise. Listeners get a sober, careful mind working on a wild subject.
podcast-tuckercarlson-D-JIqINmoSk:
Steve Baker is a journalist who was himself prosecuted over January 6 and later saw the charges dropped. He joins Tucker Carlson to argue that the official story of that day still hides its key episode. That episode is the pipe bombs found near party headquarters. Baker also discusses the CIA, the FBI, and what he calls directed energy weapons.

The pipe bomb case remains unsolved in its public details, and Baker treats that gap as evidence of deception. Carlson, sympathetic, helps him lay out the timeline problems. Their claims go well beyond the public record and are preserved as argument, not finding. The episode's interest is partly biographical too: a man the state charged over January 6 now using a large platform to accuse the state over the same day, in detail.
the-black-mask:
E. W. Hornung's Raffles stories, first published in 1901, are introduced here through later praise for the gentleman thief. Raffles is described as a man about town and famous cricketer by day, and a master burglar by night. Stories listed include No Sinecure and A Jubilee Present.

An opening account says Hornung, who married Arthur Conan Doyle's sister, inverted Holmes and Watson into Raffles and Bunny, living by stealing. Doyle is quoted calling the tales fine short-story writing but dangerous in making a criminal a hero. The first story opens on May 11, 1897, with a telegram about an advertisement surprising the narrator.
the-brown-mask: Percy J. Brebner wrote The Brown Mask, dated 1911. Brebner had also written Princess Maritza, Vayenne, and A Royal Ward. The chapters, thirty, start with Brethren of the Road and Barbara Lanison. Grey Eyes, The Nun of Aylingford, and Children of the Devil come next. Mad Martin, King Monmouth, and Sedgemoor and Afterwards turn the tale to war. Lord Rosmore dictates terms in one, and takes the luck in the next. The triple alliance, a flight, a leather case, and Safety close the list. No tale page is shown.
the-cask: The Cask, by Freeman Wills Crofts, dated 1920, appears here as Volume 25 of The Crime Club, presented through the publisher's own pages. A blurb headed This is the Story makes large claims. The book, it says, introduced a new master of detective fiction. It offers a mysterious murder cunningly conceived. Suspicion is ingeniously thrown on an innocent man. A subtle alibi is brilliantly shattered by an unfaltering process of analysis. The design is called flawless. No page of the novel is shown.
the-face-and-the-mask:
Robert Barr gathered twenty-four tales in The Face and the Mask, a book of short fiction with a wry bent. Story heads in the contents range from The Woman of Stone to The Great Pegram Mystery and The Doom of London.

Crime, tricks, and odd turns drive the set. One tale deals with the making of a new explosive, another with marked cards, and others with a raid, a bruiser's courtship, and a man changed in strange ways. Barr mixes mystery with humor, and most tales turn on a secret face worn over a real one.
to-be-read-at-dusk:
Charles Dickens's story appears in a 1905 Chapman and Hall edition of his works, issued also by Scribner's in New York. Five couriers sit on a bench outside a convent atop the Great St. Bernard in Switzerland. Sunset stains the remote heights like red wine spilt on snow.

The German courier coined that simile, Dickens notes, while a shed nearby holds travellers' bodies dug from snow, preserved by cold. Wind rises, coats button, and talk resumes after the sublime sight stops it. An American gentleman indoors has been recounting a fortune's accumulation. Readers get a framed tale told among Alpine couriers.
tom-swift-and-his-air-scout-or-uncle-sam: Uncle Sam's Mastery of the Sky is promised in the Tom Swift air scout story by Victor Appleton, laid out in twenty-five chapter headings. A sky ride, a big government offer, a problem in sound, a spy chase, and a deserted cabin appear in sequence. Chapter one opens with a companion asking Tom whether the ride is really safe, then stops. The contents and that opening question are what is shown in this record, so Appleton's aviation story itself does not appear beyond them.
